pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l01.q: A patient has had 60 cm of terminal ileum resected for Crohn disease. Which two deficiencies should be anticipated?
choices: Iron and folate
Vitamin B12 and bile salt recycling
Amylase and pepsin
Vitamin K and calcium only
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l01.why: The ileum is the only site that absorbs intrinsic-factor-bound B12 and the only site that recycles bile salts, so losing it costs both. Iron, calcium and folate are duodenal, and enzymes are secreted rather than absorbed.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l01.q: About 1 to 1.5 L of liquid chyme enters the colon daily. Roughly how much leaves as stool, and what does that tell you about a patient with high-output diarrhea?
choices: 100 to 200 mL, so losing colonic function causes rapid dehydration
About 1 L, so colonic water handling is minor
About 50 mL, and diarrhea has no volume consequence
About 700 mL, and the small bowel does the reclaiming
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l01.why: The colon reclaims nearly all of the liquid arriving, leaving 100 to 200 mL of stool, so a patient who loses that step dehydrates quickly and should be assessed for orthostatic changes. Most absorption of nutrients, though not this final water reclamation, happens in the small bowel.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l02.q: Why does a drug taken orally often reach the bloodstream at a much lower concentration than the same dose given intravenously?
choices: Stomach acid destroys all oral drugs
Roughly 75 percent of liver blood arrives by the portal vein, so absorbed drug passes through the liver and is metabolized before reaching the systemic circulation
Oral drugs are absorbed by the colon only
The small intestine actively excretes drugs back into the lumen
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l02.why: Portal blood carries everything absorbed to the liver first, where cytochrome P450 enzymes metabolize a fraction of it, which is first-pass metabolism. Acid degradation affects some drugs but does not explain the general phenomenon.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l02.q: A patient has right upper quadrant pain, a temperature of 38.9 C and a total bilirubin of 5.8 mg/dL. Where is the stone and what is the diagnosis?
choices: Cystic duct; cholecystitis
Common bile duct; ascending cholangitis
Pancreatic duct only; chronic pancreatitis
Ampulla of Vater; simple biliary colic
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l02.why: Pain plus jaundice plus fever is Charcot's triad, meaning an obstructed and infected common bile duct, which is a drainage emergency. A cystic duct stone inflames the gallbladder without jaundice, and biliary colic has neither fever nor jaundice.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l03.q: Why is early appendicitis pain felt around the umbilicus rather than in the right lower quadrant?
choices: The appendix begins in the midline and migrates later in life
Visceral afferents report to the spinal segment the organ developed from, around T10, giving vague midline pain until the parietal peritoneum is involved
The appendix shares innervation with the bladder
Referred pain always presents in the midline
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l03.why: Hollow organ afferents are sparse and map to the embryologic segment, producing dull poorly localized midline pain; once inflammation reaches the somatically innervated parietal peritoneum the pain sharpens and localizes to McBurney's point. The appendix does not migrate in adulthood.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l03.q: Pressing on the left lower quadrant produces pain in the right lower quadrant. What is this sign called and what does it support?
choices: Murphy's sign, supporting cholecystitis
Rovsing's sign, supporting appendicitis
Kehr's sign, supporting splenic injury
Cullen's sign, supporting retroperitoneal bleeding
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l03.why: Rovsing's sign transmits pressure across the peritoneum to the inflamed right lower quadrant and supports appendicitis. Murphy's sign is an inspiratory arrest under the right costal margin, Kehr's is referred left shoulder pain, and Cullen's is periumbilical bruising.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l04.q: A patient with a small bowel obstruction has vomited only twice but has a blood pressure of 92/58 and a heart rate of 118. How can he be volume depleted?
choices: The vomiting alone explains it
Fluid has poured into the distended bowel lumen instead of returning to the blood, which is third spacing
Obstruction causes an immediate bone marrow failure
He must have an undiagnosed GI bleed
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l04.why: In obstruction the bowel wall swells and secretions accumulate in the lumen, so litres can be lost from the circulation without ever leaving the body. That is why obstructed patients need aggressive resuscitation even before significant vomiting.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l04.q: Which combination of vomiting pattern and obstipation timing points to a LARGE bowel obstruction?
choices: Early bilious vomiting with late obstipation
Late feculent vomiting with early obstipation and marked distension
Early feculent vomiting with no distension
No vomiting and no obstipation
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l04.why: A distal block allows a long column of bowel to fill, so gas and stool stop early while vomiting comes late and is feculent, with marked distension. Small bowel obstruction reverses that pattern with early bilious vomiting and later obstipation.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l05.q: Roughly 180 L is filtered at the glomerulus each day and 1 to 2 L is voided. What does that comparison tell you about tubular function?
choices: More than 99 percent of the filtrate is reabsorbed downstream
About 50 percent is reabsorbed
The glomerulus filters only waste
The numbers indicate glomerular disease
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l05.why: Reclaiming over 99 percent of the filtrate is the normal job of the tubules and collecting ducts, which is why tubular injury produces such dramatic fluid and electrolyte consequences. The glomerulus filters plasma indiscriminately apart from cells and large proteins.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l05.q: A patient on spironolactone, lisinopril and a potassium supplement has an eGFR of 28. What is the risk?
choices: Severe hypokalemia requiring more supplementation
Lethal hyperkalemia, because all three raise potassium and the kidney cannot excrete the load
Hypernatremia from aldosterone blockade
Metabolic alkalosis from ACE inhibition
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l05.why: Spironolactone blocks aldosterone at the collecting duct, ACE inhibition lowers aldosterone, and the supplement adds potassium directly, so a failing kidney cannot compensate. This exact combination appears frequently on real medication lists.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l06.q: A 70 kg man receives 1 L of 0.9 percent normal saline. Approximately how much remains in the vascular space after equilibration?
choices: About 250 mL, since isotonic fluid distributes through the extracellular space
The full 1000 mL
About 80 mL
About 660 mL
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l06.why: Isotonic crystalloid stays in the extracellular compartment, which is about three quarters interstitial and one quarter plasma, so roughly a quarter remains intravascular. D5W behaves as free water and leaves only about one twelfth in the vessels.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l06.q: Which statement correctly separates the two questions a clinician must ask about fluid status?
choices: Serum sodium reports total body salt and blood pressure reports osmolality
Serum sodium answers a water question, while blood pressure, heart rate, urine output and jugular veins answer the volume question
Both questions are answered by the serum sodium alone
Urine output reports osmolality
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l06.why: Sodium concentration reflects the ratio of water to solute, so it is a water problem, while perfusion signs report the adequacy of the extracellular volume. A patient can have a perfectly normal sodium and be profoundly volume depleted.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l07.q: A patient's serum sodium of 112 mEq/L is corrected to 126 mEq/L over 18 hours. What complication is now a risk?
choices: Cerebral edema from overly slow correction
Osmotic demyelination from correction faster than 8 to 10 mEq/L in 24 hours
Hypernatremic seizures
Immediate rebound hyponatremia
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l07.why: A 14 mEq/L rise in 18 hours far exceeds the 8 to 10 mEq/L daily ceiling, risking permanent brainstem injury from osmotic demyelination. Cerebral edema is the risk of correcting hypernatremia too fast, not hyponatremia too fast.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l07.q: Which hyperkalemia treatment actually REMOVES potassium from the body?
choices: Calcium gluconate
Regular insulin with dextrose
Nebulized albuterol
Dialysis
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l07.why: Calcium stabilizes the membrane and insulin and albuterol shift potassium into cells temporarily, but only diuresis, binders and dialysis remove it, and dialysis is definitive in renal failure. Relying on shifting agents alone lets the potassium return within hours.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l08.q: A 78-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia has made no urine for 10 hours and has a creatinine of 3.1 mg/dL. What is the first diagnostic step?
choices: A 2 L fluid bolus
A bladder scan, because post-renal obstruction is the fastest cause to confirm and reverse
Urgent dialysis
A renal biopsy
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l08.why: Obstruction is the most rapidly reversible cause of acute kidney injury and a bladder scan plus a catheter can restore urine output in minutes. Fluids and dialysis address the wrong mechanism and a biopsy is never the first step.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l08.q: Which laboratory pattern fits acute tubular necrosis rather than a pre-renal state?
choices: BUN to creatinine ratio above 20:1 with concentrated urine and low urine sodium
BUN to creatinine ratio around 10 to 15:1 with muddy brown granular casts and higher urine sodium
Normal urinalysis with a ratio of 30:1
Absent urine sodium with hyaline casts only
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l08.why: Damaged tubules cannot hoard sodium or concentrate urine, so the ratio falls toward 10 to 15:1, urine sodium rises, and muddy brown granular casts appear. The hoarding pattern with a ratio above 20:1 and low urine sodium is the pre-renal kidney working correctly.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l09.q: A patient has a suppressed TSH with an elevated free T4. What does this pattern indicate about the source of the problem?
choices: The pituitary is failing to stimulate a normal thyroid
The thyroid is producing hormone independently, and the pituitary is correctly shutting off
The hypothalamus is over-producing TRH
The result is internally inconsistent
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l09.why: High final hormone with a low stimulating hormone means the target gland is running autonomously and negative feedback is intact, as in Graves disease. A failing gland would show a high TSH with a low T4.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l09.q: Which hormones does the POSTERIOR pituitary release, and where are they made?
choices: TSH and ACTH, made in the posterior pituitary
ADH and oxytocin, made in the hypothalamus and stored posteriorly
Cortisol and aldosterone, made in the adrenal cortex
Prolactin and growth hormone, made in the posterior lobe
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l09.why: The posterior pituitary is a storage and release terminal for hypothalamic ADH and oxytocin and manufactures nothing. TSH, ACTH, prolactin and growth hormone are anterior pituitary products.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l10.q: A DKA patient's potassium reads 5.4 mEq/L on arrival. What is actually true about total body potassium?
choices: It is elevated to match the serum level
It is profoundly depleted, because osmotic diuresis has been dumping potassium for hours while acidosis shifted it out of cells
It is normal, and no replacement will be needed
It cannot be assessed without a 24-hour urine
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l10.why: Acidosis drives potassium out of cells so the serum reads normal or high, while hours of osmotic diuresis have emptied the body stores, which is why the level crashes once insulin starts. Replacement is planned from the outset rather than deferred.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l10.q: Why does HHS produce little or no ketosis despite glucose levels above 600 mg/dL?
choices: Type 2 patients cannot make ketones at all
Residual circulating insulin is still enough to suppress lipolysis, even though it cannot control glucose
The kidney clears ketones faster in HHS
Hyperosmolality chemically destroys ketones
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l10.why: Even a small amount of insulin blocks lipolysis, so fat is not mobilized into ketoacids, which is why HHS presents with dehydration and altered mentation rather than air hunger. The absent ketosis is about residual insulin, not clearance or chemistry.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l11.q: A patient has HBsAg positive, anti-HBc IgM positive and anti-HBs negative. How is this interpreted?
choices: Vaccinated, not infected
Acute hepatitis B infection, currently infectious
Resolved infection with immunity
Chronic hepatitis C
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l11.why: Surface antigen means virus is present and infectious, and an IgM core antibody dates the infection as acute or recent, with no protective surface antibody yet. Vaccination produces isolated anti-HBs with a negative core antibody.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l11.q: A patient presents 30 hours after a large acetaminophen ingestion with an ALT of 4,200 U/L and an INR of 2.4. Should N-acetylcysteine still be given?
choices: No, it is only useful within 8 hours
Yes, it is still given late because it benefits patients even in established liver injury
No, only transplant evaluation matters now
Only if the 4-hour level was above the nomogram line
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l11.why: NAC is nearly 100 percent hepatoprotective within 8 hours but is still given late because it improves outcomes in established hepatotoxicity and fulminant failure. A nomogram level is not obtainable or required this far out with clear injury.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l12.q: A cirrhotic with ascites needs a 7 L paracentesis. What must accompany it and why?
choices: Nothing, large volume taps need no support
Albumin about 6 to 8 g per litre removed, to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction
A litre of D5W per litre removed
Prophylactic platelets
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l12.why: Removing more than about 5 L can precipitate circulatory collapse, and albumin replacement at 6 to 8 g per litre prevents it. Dextrose water does not support intravascular volume and platelets are not routinely required.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l12.q: Which laboratory value should NOT be used to titrate lactulose in hepatic encephalopathy?
choices: Stool frequency
The serum ammonia level, which correlates poorly with grade
Serum sodium
The West Haven grade
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l12.why: Lactulose is titrated to 2 to 3 soft stools per day and the clinical grade, because the ammonia level tracks neither severity nor response. Time spent chasing the ammonia is better spent hunting the precipitant such as bleeding, infection or constipation.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l13.q: A patient with acute pancreatitis has an ALT of 240 U/L with an upper limit of normal of 40. What does this suggest about the cause?
choices: Alcohol-related pancreatitis
A gallstone cause, since an ALT more than 3 times normal points at a stone
Hypertriglyceridemia
Autoimmune pancreatitis
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l13.why: A transaminase rise above three times normal in acute pancreatitis strongly suggests biliary obstruction from a stone. Alcohol and triglyceride causes do not typically produce that pattern, and triglyceride-induced disease requires levels above 1000 mg/dL.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l13.q: Which fluid strategy is now recommended for acute pancreatitis?
choices: 250 to 500 mL/hr of normal saline for every patient for 48 hours
Moderate goal-directed lactated Ringer's, roughly 1.5 mL/kg/hr with a 10 mL/kg bolus only if hypovolemic
Strict fluid restriction
Colloid only
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l13.why: Goal-directed moderate resuscitation with lactated Ringer's, reassessed every few hours, avoids the fluid overload and respiratory failure caused by the older aggressive reflex without worsening outcomes. Restriction risks under-resuscitation, signalled by a rising BUN or hematocrit at 24 hours.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l14.q: Which feature is found in Crohn disease but NEVER in ulcerative colitis?
choices: Bloody diarrhea
Perianal fistulas and transmural strictures
Crypt abscesses on biopsy
Colorectal cancer risk with long-standing disease
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l14.why: Fistulas, strictures and abscesses follow from transmural inflammation, which is unique to Crohn disease; ulcerative colitis is limited to mucosa and submucosa. Crypt abscesses are a UC finding, and both diseases raise long-term colorectal cancer risk.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l14.q: Why must colonoscopy be deferred 6 to 8 weeks after an episode of diverticulitis rather than performed acutely?
choices: The prep is unpleasant during illness
Acute inflammation raises perforation risk, while the delayed study is done to exclude an underlying cancer
Colonoscopy cannot visualize the sigmoid
Antibiotics interfere with the optics
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l14.why: Insufflating an acutely inflamed, micro-perforated segment risks perforation, and the purpose of the delayed study is to rule out a cancer mimicking diverticulitis. CT, not colonoscopy, makes the acute diagnosis and separates complicated from uncomplicated disease.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l15.q: Why does over-transfusing a patient with a variceal bleed cause harm?
choices: It dilutes platelets below a safe level
It raises portal pressure and provokes rebleeding
It causes immediate hemolysis
It masks the hemoglobin trend
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l15.why: Restoring volume aggressively drives portal pressure back up across the varix, which is a mechanical reason the restrictive threshold of 7 g/dL performs better. Dilution and hemolysis are not the operative mechanisms here.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l15.q: A stable patient with an upper GI bleed has a Glasgow-Blatchford score of 0. What does this permit?
choices: Immediate discharge with no follow-up of any kind
Consideration of outpatient management without inpatient endoscopy
Mandatory intensive care admission
Immediate TIPS
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l15.why: A score of 0 to 1 identifies a very low-risk bleed that can often be managed as an outpatient without inpatient endoscopy, though arranged follow-up remains part of the plan. TIPS and intensive care are for high-risk or refractory variceal bleeding.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l16.q: Why does a closed-loop obstruction strangulate faster than a simple obstruction?
choices: It involves only the colon
The segment is blocked at two points and cannot decompress in either direction
It always occurs in the stomach
It responds poorly to antibiotics
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l16.why: With both ends blocked the trapped segment has no route to decompress, so pressure rises quickly and cuts off its own blood supply. A simple obstruction can at least vent proximally through vomiting or a nasogastric tube.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l16.q: Before giving neostigmine 2 mg IV for acute colonic pseudo-obstruction, what must be at the bedside?
choices: Atropine and continuous cardiac monitoring, because profound bradycardia is the expected hazard
Naloxone and a bag-valve mask
Calcium gluconate
Flumazenil
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l16.why: Neostigmine is a cholinesterase inhibitor that can produce marked bradycardia, so atropine and monitoring are mandatory. Naloxone, calcium and flumazenil address entirely different drug classes.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l17.q: A patient with acute kidney injury who takes furosemide has a FENa of 2.8 percent. What should be done with this result?
choices: Conclude acute tubular necrosis
Disregard it, because diuretics force sodium out regardless, and use a fractional excretion of urea under 35 percent to identify a pre-renal state
Conclude a pre-renal state
Repeat the FENa in one hour
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l17.why: Loop diuretics invalidate the FENa by forcing sodium excretion no matter the underlying physiology, so the urea-based fraction is substituted. Repeating the same invalid test changes nothing.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l17.q: A patient with rhabdomyolysis has an ionized calcium of 3.8 mg/dL and no tetany or ECG changes. What is the correct approach to the calcium?
choices: Give calcium gluconate immediately to normalize it
Withhold calcium unless symptomatic or there are hyperkalemic ECG changes, because calcium returns as hypercalcemia during recovery
Give oral calcium and vitamin D
Start dialysis for the calcium alone
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l17.why: Calcium deposits into damaged muscle early and is released back later, so replacing it in an asymptomatic patient sets up rebound hypercalcemia. Treatment focuses on aggressive isotonic fluid targeting 200 to 300 mL/hr of urine.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l18.q: A patient has a bicarbonate of 10 mEq/L and a measured pCO2 of 34 mmHg. Using Winter's formula, what does this indicate?
choices: Appropriate respiratory compensation
The expected pCO2 is about 23, so a measured 34 means a superimposed respiratory acidosis and a tiring patient
A primary respiratory alkalosis
A normal acid-base status
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l18.why: Winter's formula gives an expected pCO2 of 1.5 x 10 + 8, about 23 plus or minus 2, so a pCO2 of 34 is far too high and signals failing ventilation on top of the metabolic acidosis. A pCO2 lower than expected would suggest an added respiratory alkalosis.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l18.q: A patient has a measured serum osmolality of 318 and a calculated osmolality of 288 mOsm/kg, with a wide anion gap and a normal lactate. What does the gap of 30 suggest?
choices: Laboratory error
An unmeasured small molecule such as methanol or ethylene glycol
Severe hyperglycemia alone
Dehydration
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l18.why: An osmolar gap over 10 mOsm/kg means an osmotically active molecule not in the calculation, and a toxic alcohol is the concern when the gap acidosis has no lactate or ketones. Glucose and BUN are already part of the calculated value, so hyperglycemia and dehydration do not create the gap.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l19.q: Why is hydrocortisone given BEFORE levothyroxine in myxedema coma?
choices: Levothyroxine is inactive without cortisol
Coexisting adrenal insufficiency is common, and thyroid hormone accelerates cortisol metabolism, which can precipitate adrenal crisis
Hydrocortisone lowers the TSH faster
Levothyroxine cannot be given intravenously
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l19.why: Replacing thyroid hormone first speeds cortisol clearance in a patient who may already be adrenally insufficient, tipping them into crisis. Levothyroxine is given intravenously at 200 to 400 mcg as a load after the steroid.

pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l19.q: A DKA patient meets resolution criteria and the infusion is about to stop. What must happen first?
choices: Nothing, the infusion can simply be stopped
Long-acting subcutaneous insulin is given 1 to 2 hours before stopping the drip, or the anion gap reopens
The patient must eat a full meal
Bicarbonate must be given
pa-anatomy-gi-renal-endo-l19.why: Intravenous insulin has a half-life of minutes, so basal coverage must already be circulating before the infusion stops or ketogenesis restarts within hours. Bicarbonate is reserved for a pH below 6.9 and eating is not a substitute for basal insulin.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old with dementia is fed thin liquids and repeatedly develops right lower lobe pneumonia. Which phase of swallowing is failing and why does the right lower lobe suffer?
choices: Oral phase; the tongue cannot form a bolus
Pharyngeal phase; the epiglottis fails to cover the larynx and the right mainstem bronchus is more vertical
Esophageal phase; peristalsis is absent
None; recurrent pneumonia is unrelated to swallowing
quiz.why: The involuntary pharyngeal phase protects the airway, and when it is blunted by dementia, stroke or sedation material enters the trachea, preferentially down the straighter right mainstem. Oral and esophageal phase problems cause drooling or dysphagia rather than aspiration pneumonia.

quiz.q: After a total gastrectomy, which deficiency is inevitable without supplementation, and why?
choices: Iron, because the duodenum is removed
Vitamin B12, because parietal cells that make intrinsic factor are gone
Vitamin C, because acid is required for absorption
Vitamin K, because colonic bacteria are eliminated
quiz.why: Parietal cells make both hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, and without intrinsic factor the ileum cannot absorb B12 regardless of intake. The duodenum and colon remain intact after gastrectomy.

quiz.q: Which structure has the greatest absorptive surface area, and approximately how large is it?
choices: The stomach, about 1 square meter
The small intestine, about 250 square meters from folds, villi and microvilli
The colon, about 100 square meters
The esophagus, about 10 square meters
quiz.why: Circular folds, villi and microvilli amplify the roughly 6 m small intestine to about 250 square meters, which is why it does nearly all nutrient absorption. The stomach mainly mixes and secretes, and the colon reclaims water.

quiz.q: A cirrhotic patient has an albumin of 1.8 g/dL, an INR of 2.3 and a total bilirubin of 4.6 mg/dL. Which liver functions have failed, in order of the findings?
choices: Albumin synthesis, clotting factor synthesis and bilirubin conjugation
Ammonia conversion, bile storage and glycogen release
Drug metabolism only
Portal blood filtration only
quiz.why: Each abnormality maps to a lost hepatic job: low albumin lets fluid leave vessels and causes ascites, a rising INR reflects lost synthesis of factors II, V, VII, IX and X, and jaundice reflects failed bilirubin conjugation. Bile is stored by the gallbladder rather than the liver.

quiz.q: A trauma patient with a left-sided rib 9 to 11 injury is hypotensive and complains of left shoulder pain. Which organ is most likely injured and what is the sign called?
choices: Liver; Murphy's sign
Spleen; Kehr's sign
Left kidney; Grey Turner's sign
Pancreas; Cullen's sign
quiz.why: The spleen sits behind ribs 9 to 11 and is the organ most often injured in blunt abdominal trauma, and blood under the left diaphragm irritates the phrenic nerve to refer pain to the left shoulder, which is Kehr's sign. Grey Turner and Cullen signs are late bruising patterns of retroperitoneal bleeding.

quiz.q: Why are pancreatic digestive enzymes secreted in an inactive form?
choices: Because they require bile to be synthesized
Because active enzymes would digest the pancreas itself, which is exactly what happens in pancreatitis
Because the duodenum destroys active enzymes
Because the liver activates them during first-pass metabolism
quiz.why: Zymogens are switched on in the duodenum, and premature intrapancreatic activation is the core mechanism of pancreatitis, most often triggered by gallstones or alcohol. Bile emulsifies fat rather than synthesizing enzymes.

quiz.q: A 58-year-old has severe epigastric pain that he describes as boring straight through to his back. Which anatomic fact explains that radiation?
choices: The stomach lies against the diaphragm
The pancreas is retroperitoneal, so inflammation involves posterior structures directly
The gallbladder shares innervation with the scapula
The appendix refers to the back
quiz.why: The pancreas sits behind the peritoneum against the posterior abdominal wall, so its inflammation projects to the back. Gallbladder pain refers to the right shoulder or scapula and appendicitis to the periumbilical region, not the back.

quiz.q: A patient with epigastric pain, nausea and diaphoresis is diagnosed with gastritis after symptoms improve with an antacid. What critical error may have occurred?
choices: None; antacid response confirms a gastric cause
An inferior wall myocardial infarction can present as epigastric pain, and symptomatic relief from antacids does not exclude it
Gastritis cannot cause diaphoresis
The patient likely has appendicitis
quiz.why: Inferior wall infarction shares T1 to T4 afferent input with the epigastrium, and response to antacids has no diagnostic value. This is precisely why epigastric pain is never filed under indigestion without considering the heart.

quiz.q: A 31-year-old woman has right lower quadrant pain. Which structures in that quadrant must be considered besides the appendix?
choices: Spleen and pancreas tail
Right ovary and tube, cecum, and right ureter
Sigmoid colon and left ureter
Gallbladder and duodenum
quiz.why: The right lower quadrant holds the appendix, cecum, right adnexa and right ureter, so ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion and ureteral stone all belong in the differential. The spleen and pancreatic tail are left upper, the sigmoid is left lower, and the gallbladder is right upper.

quiz.q: Two patients have abdominal pain. One lies rigidly still and resists any movement of the stretcher; the other cannot stop shifting position. What does each posture suggest?
choices: The still patient has colic and the restless patient has peritonitis
The still patient has peritoneal inflammation and the restless patient has a squeezing hollow organ such as a stone or early obstruction
Both suggest peritonitis
Posture carries no diagnostic information
quiz.why: Peritoneal inflammation is aggravated by any movement dragging inflamed surfaces, so those patients lie motionless, while colicky visceral pain gives no position of relief and produces writhing. The distinction is made before a single lab returns.

quiz.q: A patient with a bowel obstruction whose bowel sounds were high-pitched and tinkling now has a silent abdomen with constant pain, a temperature of 38.7 C and a heart rate of 126. What has happened?
choices: The obstruction has resolved
Strangulation, meaning the blood supply has been compromised and bowel is dying
A simple ileus has developed
The patient has developed gastroenteritis
quiz.why: The shift from crampy to constant pain with fever, tachycardia and a silent abdomen marks strangulation, which kills bowel within hours. Resolution would bring passage of flatus and relief rather than systemic signs.

quiz.q: Roughly how much blood and how much time are required to produce melena?
choices: About 50 mL and roughly 14 hours of transit
About 500 mL and 2 hours
About 10 mL and 1 hour
Melena requires at least 2 L of blood loss
quiz.why: As little as 50 mL of blood, given about 14 hours in the gut, is digested into the black tarry stool of melena. A brisk upper bleed can move too fast to blacken and instead present as hematochezia, which is a classic miss.

quiz.q: Why does a patient with a serum glucose of 420 mg/dL produce large volumes of urine?
choices: High glucose directly damages the collecting duct
Proximal tubular glucose transport saturates near 180 mg/dL, so glucose remains in the filtrate and drags water with it osmotically
Hyperglycemia suppresses aldosterone
Glucose stimulates ADH release
quiz.why: Once the transport maximum is exceeded, unreabsorbed glucose acts as an osmotic agent in the tubule and produces an osmotic diuresis that also drags out sodium and potassium. Glucose neither destroys the duct nor stimulates ADH.

quiz.q: Which nephron segment builds the concentration gradient that makes concentrated urine possible?
choices: The glomerulus
The proximal convoluted tubule
The loop of Henle, with a water-permeable descending limb and a salt-pumping waterproof ascending limb
The collecting duct alone
quiz.why: Countercurrent function in the loop creates a salty medulla, and without that gradient ADH acting on the collecting duct has nothing to pull water toward. The glomerulus filters and the proximal tubule reabsorbs in bulk without generating the gradient.

quiz.q: A patient on high-dose furosemide has a potassium of 2.9 mEq/L. Which two mechanisms explain the loss?
choices: Direct potassium excretion by the loop plus reduced dietary intake
More sodium delivered to the collecting duct to be traded for potassium, plus volume loss raising aldosterone
Reduced aldosterone plus metabolic acidosis
Potassium shifting into cells from alkalosis only
quiz.why: Loop diuretics block the thick ascending limb, so a large sodium load arrives distally where aldosterone drives sodium-potassium exchange, and the accompanying volume loss raises aldosterone further. The drug does not excrete potassium directly at the loop.

quiz.q: A 70 kg man's total body water is about 42 L. Approximately how much of that is plasma?
choices: About 3 L
About 14 L
About 28 L
About 11 L
quiz.why: Two thirds of body water is intracellular (about 28 L) and one third extracellular (about 14 L), of which roughly 11 L is interstitial and only about 3 L is plasma. That small plasma volume is why resuscitation fluid choice matters so much.

quiz.q: A patient receives 6 L of 0.9 percent normal saline during resuscitation and develops a pH of 7.29 with a chloride of 118 mEq/L and a normal anion gap. What has happened?
choices: Lactic acidosis from shock
Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis from large-volume saline
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Renal tubular acidosis from the fluid
quiz.why: Normal saline delivers 154 mEq/L of chloride, and large volumes produce a non-gap hyperchloremic acidosis, which is why balanced solutions such as lactated Ringer's are often preferred. A lactic or ketoacidosis would widen the anion gap.

quiz.q: Which patient is DEHYDRATED as opposed to volume depleted?
choices: A patient vomiting for three days with a normal sodium and flat neck veins
A nursing home resident with no access to water, a sodium of 158 mEq/L and concentrated scant urine
A trauma patient who has lost 1.5 L of blood
A burn patient with massive third spacing
quiz.why: Dehydration is loss of water alone, raising osmolality and sodium, while volume depletion is loss of salt and water together and can occur with a perfectly normal sodium. Hemorrhage and third spacing are volume problems.

quiz.q: A patient with a potassium of 7.8 mEq/L has flattened P waves and a PR of 260 ms. Where on the ECG ladder is this, and what comes next if untreated?
choices: Earliest change; nothing further will happen
Second rung; the QRS will widen, then a sine wave and ventricular fibrillation or asystole
Final rung; recovery is expected
This pattern indicates hypokalemia
quiz.why: Peaked T waves appear first around 5.5 to 6.5, flattened P waves and PR prolongation around 6.5 to 7.5, then QRS widening around 7 to 8, then sine wave and arrest. Hypokalemia produces flattened T waves and U waves instead.

quiz.q: A patient has an albumin of 2.5 g/dL and a total calcium of 7.9 mg/dL. What is the albumin-corrected calcium?
choices: About 7.9 mg/dL, no correction needed
About 9.1 mg/dL
About 6.7 mg/dL
About 10.5 mg/dL
quiz.why: Add 0.8 mg/dL for each 1 g/dL the albumin sits below 4, so 1.5 x 0.8 = 1.2, giving about 9.1 mg/dL, which is normal. Failing to correct would lead to unnecessary calcium replacement in a patient whose ionized fraction is fine.

quiz.q: A patient with hypercalcemia of 13.8 mg/dL has constipation, confusion and a history of kidney stones. Which ECG change is expected?
choices: A prolonged QT interval
A shortened QT interval
Peaked T waves
A widened QRS
quiz.why: High calcium shortens the QT while low calcium prolongs it, alongside tetany and Chvostek and Trousseau signs. Peaked T waves and a wide QRS belong to hyperkalemia.

quiz.q: A patient with a new dialysis fistula in the right arm arrives by ambulance with an IV placed in that arm and a blood pressure cuff cycling on it. What is the concern?
choices: Nothing, a mature fistula tolerates both
Clotting or damaging the access, which can send the patient to the operating room
Falsely low blood pressure readings only
Increased risk of hyperkalemia
quiz.why: No cuff, IV, tourniquet or blood draw goes in an access arm, because clotting the fistula costs the patient their dialysis access and a trip to surgery. A patent fistula should have a palpable thrill and an audible bruit.

quiz.q: A patient's eGFR is 22 mL/min/1.73 m2. What CKD stage is this, and which complications should be anticipated?
choices: Stage 3a; mild anemia only
Stage 4; anemia, bone disease, metabolic acidosis, hypertension and hyperkalemia
Stage 5; immediate dialysis is mandatory
Stage 2; no complications expected
quiz.why: Stage 4 spans 15 to 29 mL/min/1.73 m2 and brings the full set of complications from lost erythropoietin, lost vitamin D activation and lost acid and potassium excretion. Stage 5 begins below 15 or on dialysis, and dialysis is triggered by symptoms rather than a number alone.

quiz.q: A patient on peritoneal dialysis reports abdominal pain and notices that the drained fluid is cloudy. What is the concern?
choices: Normal appearance after a long dwell
Peritonitis, the characteristic emergency of peritoneal dialysis
Hypoglycemia from the dextrose in the dialysate
Catheter migration only
quiz.why: Cloudy effluent with abdominal pain is peritonitis until proven otherwise and requires prompt fluid analysis and treatment. Normal effluent is clear regardless of dwell time.

quiz.q: A patient 36 hours after total thyroidectomy has perioral tingling and carpal spasm when a blood pressure cuff is inflated. What has happened and what is the sign called?
choices: Hypocalcemia from parathyroid removal or stunning; Trousseau's sign
Hypercalcemia from bone release; Chvostek's sign
Thyroid storm; Burch-Wartofsky positivity
Hypomagnesemia; Kussmaul's sign
quiz.why: The parathyroids sit behind the thyroid and are readily removed or stunned, producing hypocalcemia within 24 to 48 hours; carpal spasm on cuff inflation is Trousseau's sign. Chvostek's sign is facial twitching on tapping the facial nerve.

quiz.q: A 44-year-old has episodic severe hypertension with pounding headache, palpitations and drenching sweats lasting 20 minutes at a time. Which diagnosis fits?
choices: Graves disease
Pheochromocytoma
Adrenal crisis
SIADH
quiz.why: Episodic catecholamine release from an adrenal medullary tumor produces the triad of headache, palpitations and diaphoresis with paroxysmal hypertension. Graves disease causes sustained hyperthyroid features, adrenal crisis causes refractory hypotension, and SIADH causes hyponatremia.

quiz.q: Which combination of findings distinguishes SIADH from diabetes insipidus?
choices: SIADH: high sodium with dilute urine; DI: low sodium with concentrated urine
SIADH: low sodium with concentrated low-volume urine; DI: high sodium with 3 to 20 L of dilute urine
Both produce a low sodium
Both produce large volumes of dilute urine
quiz.why: Too much ADH retains free water, diluting serum sodium while concentrating the urine, whereas too little ADH lets free water pour out, raising serum sodium with dilute high-volume urine. Fluid restriction treats one and desmopressin with free water treats the other.

quiz.q: A DKA patient's glucose has fallen to 195 mg/dL after 4 hours, but the anion gap is still 19. What is the correct action?
choices: Stop the insulin infusion
Add dextrose to the intravenous fluid and continue the insulin, because insulin is treating the acidosis rather than the sugar
Give a bicarbonate infusion
Switch to subcutaneous sliding-scale insulin only
quiz.why: Insulin must run until the gap closes, so dextrose is added when glucose reaches about 200 mg/dL to allow that safely. Stopping insulin reopens ketogenesis, and bicarbonate is generally reserved for a pH below 6.9.

quiz.q: A patient with type 1 diabetes has a glucose of 58 mg/dL and reports sweating, tremor and hunger. Which physiologic response is producing those symptoms?
choices: Neuroglycopenia in the cortex
Adrenergic counter-regulation, mainly epinephrine release
Ketone production
Insulin-driven potassium shift
quiz.why: Between roughly 55 and 70 mg/dL the adrenergic warning symptoms appear from epinephrine, while neuroglycopenic confusion and seizure arrive under about 50. Beta blockers erase this warning stage, which is why those patients present already confused.

quiz.q: Which set of laboratory features distinguishes HHS from DKA?
choices: Glucose often above 600 with osmolality above 320 and minimal ketones
Glucose 350 to 800 with a pH under 7.30 and a wide anion gap
Normal glucose with heavy ketonuria
Glucose above 600 with a pH of 7.05
quiz.why: HHS is defined by extreme hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality with little ketosis because residual insulin blocks lipolysis, and fluid deficits reach 8 to 12 L. DKA runs lower glucose with acidemia and a wide gap from ketoacids.

quiz.q: A patient's hepatitis panel shows HBsAg negative, anti-HBs negative and anti-HBc positive in isolation. What does the core antibody establish?
choices: The patient is vaccinated
The patient has met the actual virus at some point, since core antibody never results from vaccination
The patient has hepatitis A
The result is impossible
quiz.why: Core antibody appears only after true infection and never after vaccination, so its presence means real exposure regardless of what the other markers show. Isolated anti-HBs would indicate vaccination.

quiz.q: A patient has an AST of 2,800 U/L and an ALT of 3,100 U/L. Which causes remain on the list?
choices: Alcoholic hepatitis, fatty liver or cirrhosis
Viral hepatitis, a drug or toxin, or shock liver
Gallstone disease alone
Chronic hepatitis C in a stable patient
quiz.why: Transaminases above 1000 U/L narrow the differential to virus, drug or toxin, or ischemic shock liver. Alcohol characteristically gives an AST to ALT ratio of 2:1 or higher with an AST rarely above 300 U/L.

quiz.q: Why is the maximum daily acetaminophen dose lowered to 2 g in a patient with chronic liver disease or heavy alcohol use?
choices: Because the drug is absorbed faster
Because glutathione stores are depleted and CYP2E1 activity is increased, so NAPQI accumulates at lower doses
Because acetaminophen is renally cleared in these patients
Because alcohol blocks intestinal absorption
quiz.why: Toxicity depends on NAPQI outrunning glutathione, and chronic alcohol use both induces CYP2E1 and depletes glutathione, shifting the threshold down from the usual 4 g ceiling. Absorption and renal clearance are not the relevant factors.

quiz.q: A patient with cirrhosis has a hepatic venous pressure gradient of 14 mmHg. What does this predict?
choices: Normal portal pressure
Varices are present and above the bleeding threshold of 12 mmHg
Varices will not form until the gradient exceeds 20
The gradient has no clinical meaning
quiz.why: A normal gradient is 3 to 5 mmHg, varices form above 10 and bleed above 12, so 14 places this patient at real bleeding risk and justifies a nonselective beta blocker or band ligation. The gradient is a validated prognostic measurement.

quiz.q: Which diuretic combination and ratio is standard for cirrhotic ascites, and why?
choices: Furosemide alone at 80 mg daily
Spironolactone 100 mg with furosemide 40 mg, a ratio that keeps potassium roughly neutral
Hydrochlorothiazide with acetazolamide
Spironolactone alone at 400 mg
quiz.why: The 100 to 40 mg ratio balances the potassium-sparing effect of spironolactone against the potassium-wasting effect of furosemide, alongside sodium restriction near 2 g daily. Loop diuretic alone drives hypokalemia and worsens encephalopathy risk.

quiz.q: A cirrhotic patient's creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 2.6 mg/dL, urine sodium is very low, the sediment is bland, and there is no improvement after albumin volume expansion. What is the diagnosis?
choices: Acute tubular necrosis
Hepatorenal syndrome
Post-renal obstruction
Contrast nephropathy
quiz.why: Hepatorenal syndrome is functional renal failure from splanchnic vasodilation in advanced cirrhosis, defined by a bland sediment, avid sodium retention and no response to volume expansion, with transplantation as the definitive treatment. ATN would show muddy brown casts and higher urine sodium.

quiz.q: Which two of three criteria are sufficient to diagnose acute pancreatitis?
choices: Characteristic epigastric pain plus lipase or amylase at least 3 times the upper limit of normal
A raised amylase plus a normal CT
Any abdominal pain plus a raised white count
Imaging plus a raised bilirubin only
quiz.why: Two of three among typical pain, enzyme elevation at least three times normal, and characteristic imaging make the diagnosis, so a patient with classic pain and a lipase of 1200 needs no CT. A white count is not one of the criteria.

quiz.q: A patient with pancreatitis has a BUN of 32 mg/dL, is confused, meets 3 SIRS criteria, is 66 years old and has a pleural effusion on chest imaging. What is the BISAP score and what does it mean?
choices: Score 2, low risk
Score 5, predicting substantially higher mortality
Score 3, borderline
BISAP cannot be calculated before 48 hours
quiz.why: All five BISAP elements are present: BUN above 25, impaired mentation, SIRS of 2 or more, age over 60 and a pleural effusion, and a score of 3 or more already predicts high mortality. BISAP is calculated in the first 24 hours, unlike Ranson criteria which require 48.

quiz.q: A patient with sterile necrotizing pancreatitis looks unwell on day 3 with a fever of 38.4 C. Should prophylactic antibiotics be started?
choices: Yes, all necrotizing pancreatitis requires prophylaxis
No, antibiotics are reserved for proven or strongly suspected infected necrosis or for cholangitis
Yes, but only oral agents
Only if the lipase remains above 1000
quiz.why: Prophylactic antibiotics in sterile pancreatitis do not improve outcomes and select resistant organisms, and fever in the first week is usually inflammatory rather than infective. Infected necrosis typically declares itself at day 7 to 10 with new fever, a rising white count and sometimes gas on CT.

quiz.q: A patient with ulcerative colitis is prescribed loperamide for 10 bloody stools daily, then develops fever, tachycardia and a transverse colon of 7 cm. What happened?
choices: The loperamide correctly slowed the diarrhea with no consequence
An antimotility drug precipitated toxic megacolon, which can perforate
This is a normal ulcerative colitis flare unrelated to the drug
The colon diameter is within normal limits
quiz.why: Antimotility agents, opioids and anticholinergics all worsen toxic megacolon, defined by colonic dilation over 6 cm plus systemic toxicity. They should be stopped rather than continued in a severe colitis flare.

quiz.q: A patient with long-standing Crohn disease involving the terminal ileum develops both gallstones and calcium oxalate kidney stones. What explains this pair?
choices: Steroid therapy
Failure of ileal bile salt recycling, which changes bile composition and increases oxalate absorption
Excess dietary calcium
Colectomy
quiz.why: The ileum recycles bile salts, and losing that function makes bile lithogenic while unabsorbed fat binds calcium, leaving oxalate free to be absorbed and precipitate in the kidney. Steroids and dietary calcium do not produce this combination.

quiz.q: Which statement about irritable bowel syndrome is correct?
choices: It is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring extensive negative testing
It is a positive diagnosis made by Rome IV criteria once alarm features are absent, and carries no cancer risk
It causes crypt abscesses on biopsy
Nocturnal symptoms that wake the patient support the diagnosis
quiz.why: Rome IV requires recurrent abdominal pain at least one day a week for three months with two of three defecation-related features, and the diagnosis is made positively when alarm features such as bleeding, weight loss, anemia or nocturnal symptoms are absent. Crypt abscesses belong to ulcerative colitis.

quiz.q: A patient with a known variceal bleed is stabilized. Within what timeframe should endoscopy be performed?
choices: Within 12 hours
Within 24 hours
Within 72 hours
Only after 5 days of octreotide
quiz.why: Suspected variceal bleeding is scoped within 12 hours once the patient is stable enough, while non-variceal upper bleeding is scoped within 24 hours. Octreotide and ceftriaxone are started before the scope rather than in place of it.

quiz.q: Why is nasogastric lavage no longer recommended to distinguish upper from lower GI bleeding?
choices: It is too expensive
It is uncomfortable, misses duodenal bleeding behind a closed pylorus, and does not change management
It causes variceal rupture in most patients
It has been replaced by plain abdominal films
quiz.why: A negative lavage cannot exclude a duodenal source, and the result does not alter the decision to scope, so the discomfort buys nothing. Erythromycin before endoscopy, not lavage, is what improves the endoscopic view.

quiz.q: A patient with uncontrolled variceal bleeding has a balloon tamponade tube placed. What are the two constraints on its use?
choices: It can stay up to 7 days and needs no airway
It is a bridge for a maximum of about 24 hours and requires a secured airway
It is definitive therapy and replaces TIPS
It may only be used in lower GI bleeding
quiz.why: Balloon tamponade buys time to arrange definitive treatment such as TIPS and carries high complication rates beyond about 24 hours, and it is only placed with the airway secured. It is explicitly a bridge rather than definitive therapy.

quiz.q: A patient has a distended abdomen with gas distributed evenly throughout small and large bowel, no transition point on CT, and is three days post-laparotomy on scheduled opioids with a potassium of 3.0 mEq/L. What is the diagnosis?
choices: Adhesive small bowel obstruction
Postoperative ileus
Sigmoid volvulus
Closed-loop obstruction
quiz.why: Diffuse quiet distension with gas throughout and no transition point is ileus, driven here by surgery, opioids and hypokalemia, and treated by removing the causes. A mechanical obstruction has a transition point, and volvulus shows a characteristic twisted loop.

quiz.q: Which hernia type is most common overall, and which carries the highest strangulation risk?
choices: Direct inguinal is most common; umbilical strangulates most
Indirect inguinal is most common; femoral strangulates most
Femoral is most common; indirect strangulates most
Incisional is most common; direct strangulates most
quiz.why: Indirect inguinal hernias pass through the internal ring and are the most common hernia in both sexes, while femoral hernias, more common in women, pass through a narrow rigid opening and strangulate most often. Direct hernias are acquired defects in the canal floor.

quiz.q: A patient on a non-operative trial for adhesive small bowel obstruction has made no progress on day 5, with ongoing distension and no flatus. What should happen?
choices: Continue the trial for another week
Proceed to operative management, since the non-operative trial runs 3 to 5 days at most
Discharge with oral contrast at home
Begin total parenteral nutrition and continue observation indefinitely
quiz.why: A non-operative trial is limited to 3 to 5 days, and failure to progress is itself an operative indication alongside peritonitis, closed-loop obstruction or signs of ischemia. Extending observation risks strangulation.

quiz.q: A patient's creatinine rises from 0.9 to 3.8 mg/dL and urine output has been 0.2 mL/kg/hr for 26 hours. What KDIGO stage is this?
choices: Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 3
Cannot be staged without a baseline GFR
quiz.why: A creatinine more than tripled from baseline and urine under 0.3 mL/kg/hr for 24 hours each independently define stage 3, the stage associated with the highest mortality. Stage 1 is a 1.5 to 1.9 times rise and stage 2 a 2.0 to 2.9 times rise.

quiz.q: Which measure actually reduces contrast-associated kidney injury?
choices: N-acetylcysteine before the scan
Sodium bicarbonate infusion
Isotonic saline before and after, holding nephrotoxins, and minimizing contrast volume
Prophylactic dialysis after every contrast study
quiz.why: Volume expansion with isotonic saline, holding NSAIDs and other nephrotoxins, and limiting contrast load are the interventions that hold up, while N-acetylcysteine and bicarbonate infusions have not in good trials. Metformin is held with an eGFR under 30 because of lactic acidosis risk, not kidney toxicity.

quiz.q: A patient with an obstructing 8 mm ureteral stone has a temperature of 39.1 C, pyuria and hydronephrosis. What does this combination require?
choices: Tamsulosin and outpatient follow-up
Same-day decompression with a ureteral stent or nephrostomy plus antibiotics
Oral antibiotics with reassessment in 48 hours
Observation, since most stones under 10 mm pass
quiz.why: An obstructed infected kidney is a closed space filled with pus, and antibiotics cannot sterilize it without drainage, so decompression happens the same day. Medical expulsive therapy and observation apply only to uninfected stones.

quiz.q: After catheterization for urinary retention, a patient produces 260 mL/hr of urine for four consecutive hours. What is this and how is it managed?
choices: Normal diuresis; no action needed
Post-obstructive diuresis; replace roughly half the losses with isotonic fluid and follow electrolytes
Diabetes insipidus; give desmopressin
Over-drainage from the catheter; clamp it intermittently
quiz.why: Post-obstructive diuresis follows relief of obstruction and needs partial replacement with electrolyte monitoring rather than full matching, which perpetuates it. Intermittent clamping is outdated teaching and the bladder should be drained fully.

quiz.q: A patient with profuse diarrhea has a pH of 7.26, bicarbonate 15 mEq/L and an anion gap of 9. What type of acidosis is this and what supports the gut as the source?
choices: Wide anion gap acidosis; an osmolar gap confirms it
Normal anion gap acidosis from bicarbonate loss in stool, supported by a negative urine anion gap
Respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
quiz.why: Losing bicarbonate through the gut produces a hyperchloremic normal-gap acidosis, and a negative urine anion gap indicates the kidney is appropriately excreting ammonium, pointing away from renal tubular acidosis. A wide gap would suggest added acid such as ketones, lactate or a toxic alcohol.

quiz.q: A seizing patient has a sodium of 106 mEq/L. What is the correct immediate treatment and the 24-hour ceiling?
choices: Fluid restriction alone, with no sodium ceiling
3 percent saline in 100 mL boluses, up to three, targeting a 4 to 6 mEq/L rise, with the total 24-hour rise capped at about 8 mEq/L
Normal saline at 250 mL/hr with no ceiling
Desmopressin to raise the sodium
quiz.why: An actively seizing patient is the one exception to slow correction and receives small hypertonic boluses to buy a few points fast, but the 24-hour rise is still capped to prevent osmotic demyelination. Fluid restriction alone is for the asymptomatic SIADH patient, and desmopressin would worsen the hyponatremia.

quiz.q: A patient vomiting for four days has a bicarbonate of 38, a chloride of 84 and a potassium of 2.8 mEq/L. Which single component of treatment allows the kidney to unload the excess bicarbonate?
choices: Free water
Chloride, given as normal saline with potassium chloride
Acetazolamide alone
Bicarbonate restriction in the diet
quiz.why: A chloride-depleted kidney cannot excrete bicarbonate, so replacing chloride with saline and potassium chloride is what corrects the alkalosis. Free water does not supply chloride and dietary measures are irrelevant in an acute alkalosis.

quiz.q: A patient with a suspected adrenal crisis is crashing, and the team wants to preserve a cosyntropin stimulation test. What is the correct approach?
choices: Delay all steroid until the cortisol level is drawn and the test completed
Give dexamethasone 4 mg IV, which treats the patient without interfering with the cosyntropin test
Give hydrocortisone and cancel the test permanently
Give fludrocortisone alone
quiz.why: Dexamethasone provides glucocorticoid activity without being measured in the cortisol assay, so the diagnostic test can still be performed; hydrocortisone 100 mg IV remains the standard when the test is not a concern. Delaying steroid in a crashing patient risks death.

quiz.q: Why is aspirin the wrong antipyretic in thyroid storm?
choices: It causes gastric bleeding in all hyperthyroid patients
It displaces thyroid hormone from binding proteins and raises the free hormone level
It blocks propylthiouracil absorption
It prolongs the QT interval
quiz.why: Salicylates compete for thyroid hormone binding sites, increasing free T4 and T3 exactly when hormone effect must be reduced, so acetaminophen and external cooling are used instead. The treatment sequence is beta blocker, thionamide, iodine at least an hour later, hydrocortisone and cooling.
